title: Philosophy of science
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study how science works and what it tells us about reality: the demarcation problem and falsification, confirmation and the paradoxes of induction, Bayesian confirmation, explanation, Kuhn and scientific revolutions, Lakatos and Feyerabend, scientific realism and anti-realism, underdetermination and structural realism, reduction and emergence, and values in science.
primary_reading: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: articles on the philosophy of science (free)

weeks.1: What is science? The demarcation problem
weeks.3: Confirmation, induction and the raven paradox
weeks.5: Explanation: the covering-law model and its rivals
weeks.7: Lakatos, Feyerabend and the rationality of science
weeks.8: Scientific realism and the no-miracles argument
weeks.9: Anti-realism: constructive empiricism and the pessimistic induction
weeks.11: Reduction, emergence and the special sciences
weeks.12: Values, objectivity and science in society

blocks.deliverable: Compute Bayesian updates for three pieces of evidence.
Analyze a historical theory change with Kuhn's concepts.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct the no-miracles argument.
Write a three-page essay on scientific realism.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Case study in the philosophy of science: choose a historical episode (the Copernican revolution, the discovery of oxygen, continental drift or the acceptance of atoms), describe it accurately from reliable sources, and write a 2,500-word paper that uses it to test one view from the course (falsificationism, Kuhn, Bayesianism or scientific realism).
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
